stem: When making a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base, why is the base added **in excess**?

options.rationale: An insoluble base cannot make the solution alkaline; any excess simply stays as a solid.

options.content: so that the excess base crystallises with the salt
options.rationale: The excess is removed by filtering so that it does not contaminate the salt.
Crystal size depends on how slowly the solution cools, not on the excess.

options.content: to make sure that all of the acid reacts
options.rationale: Then no acid is left to contaminate the salt, and the excess base is easily filtered off.

explanation: Adding the insoluble solid until some is left over guarantees that all the acid has been used up. The unreacted solid is then removed by filtration, leaving only the salt in solution.

stem: Which technique removes the excess copper(II) oxide from the copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.rationale: Crystallisation is used later to obtain the salt from the solution.
The insoluble solid stays on the filter paper; the salt solution passes through.
Distillation separates a liquid from a solution; it would leave the solid and salt together.
Chromatography separates dissolved substances such as dyes.

explanation: Excess insoluble solid is removed by filtration. The filtrate is the salt solution, which is then crystallised.

stem: True or false: copper(II) sulfate can be made by adding copper metal to dilute sulfuric acid.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not quite: copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute sulfuric acid. Use copper(II) oxide or copper(II) carbonate.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: copper does not react with dilute sulfuric acid. Copper(II) oxide or carbonate is used instead.

explanation: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so it cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Copper(II) sulfate is made by adding excess copper(II) oxide or copper(II) carbonate to dilute sulfuric acid.

stem: Which pair of reagents is best for making zinc sulfate crystals?

options.rationale: Dissolving zinc chloride makes zinc chloride solution; no sulfate is present.

options.content: zinc oxide and dilute hydrochloric acid
options.rationale: Hydrochloric acid would give zinc chloride, not zinc sulfate.
Zinc is less reactive than sodium, so it cannot displace sodium; no zinc sulfate forms.

options.content: zinc carbonate and dilute sulfuric acid
options.rationale: An insoluble carbonate with the acid whose anion is in the salt.

explanation: The salt contains zinc ions and sulfate ions, so react a zinc compound with sulfuric acid: $\ce{ZnCO3 + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2O + CO2}$. Add the carbonate in excess, filter and crystallise.

stem: Which salt should be prepared by the **titration** method?

options.rationale: Made from excess zinc, zinc oxide or zinc carbonate, then filtering.
Made from excess insoluble copper(II) oxide or carbonate, then filtering.
Made from excess magnesium, magnesium oxide or magnesium carbonate, then filtering.
Potassium salts are made from a soluble alkali (potassium hydroxide), so exact volumes are needed.

explanation: Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are made by titrating an acid with an alkali, because an excess of a soluble alkali could not be filtered off.

stem: Black copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid. How does the student know when the copper(II) oxide is in **excess**?

options.content: The solution turns a deep red colour.
options.rationale: Nothing red forms; copper(II) sulfate solution is blue.

options.content: Black solid stays undissolved even after stirring.
options.rationale: No more can react because all the acid has been used up.

options.content: The fizzing stops and no more gas forms at the surface.
options.rationale: Copper(II) oxide does not fizz with acid; fizzing happens with metals and carbonates.
The solution becomes blue as copper(II) sulfate forms.

explanation: When all the acid has reacted, extra copper(II) oxide has nothing to react with, so black solid stays in the blue solution.

stem: How can you tell that a hot salt solution has reached its **crystallisation point**?

options.content: The solution starts to boil steadily in the dish.
options.rationale: Boiling shows the temperature, not saturation.

options.content: The solution changes to a deeper colour as it cools.
options.rationale: The colour of the salt solution does not change at the crystallisation point.

options.content: Crystals form on a glass rod dipped in it and left to cool.
options.rationale: This shows that the solution is saturated and will crystallise on cooling.

options.content: All of the water has boiled away from the evaporating dish.
options.rationale: That is evaporating to dryness, which is avoided.

explanation: Dip a glass rod into the hot solution and let it cool in the air. If small crystals form on the rod, the solution is saturated and can be left to cool and crystallise.

stem: Why is the copper(II) sulfate solution **not** evaporated to dryness?

options.content: The copper(II) sulfate would turn back into sulfuric acid.
options.rationale: Heating does not reverse the neutralisation.

options.content: The crystals would lose their water of crystallisation.
options.rationale: Crystallising from a saturated solution keeps the water of crystallisation.

options.content: Evaporating to dryness is far too slow.
options.rationale: Speed is not the reason; the product would be impure and lose water.

options.content: The crystals would redissolve in the hot dish.
options.rationale: Without water, nothing can redissolve; the problem is losing the water of crystallisation.

explanation: Copper(II) sulfate crystals are hydrated, CuSO₄·5H₂O. Heating to dryness drives off this water (and can decompose the salt), and any soluble impurities stay mixed with the solid. Cooling a saturated solution gives purer hydrated crystals.
hints: Think about the water inside blue copper(II) sulfate crystals.

stem: Complete the final stages of preparing magnesium chloride crystals from excess magnesium oxide and dilute hydrochloric acid.

payload.template: The excess magnesium oxide is removed by {{blank:a}}. The filtrate is heated until it reaches the {{blank:b}}, then left to cool. The crystals are washed with a little cold {{blank:c}} and dried {{blank:d}}.

explanation: Filter off the excess solid; heat the filtrate to the crystallisation point; cool; wash the crystals with a little cold distilled water (which contains no dissolved impurities); dry them between filter papers or in a warm place.

stem: Match each salt with the best pair of starting materials for preparing it.

right.content: copper(II) carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid
sodium hydroxide solution and dilute sulfuric acid (titration)
magnesium oxide and dilute nitric acid

explanation: Each salt needs a source of its metal ion and the acid that supplies its anion. Sodium salts are made by titration. Silver does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid (and silver chloride is insoluble), so the last pair is not useful.
hints: Match the metal and the acid to the name of the salt.

stem: Potassium sulfate is made by titrating potassium hydroxide solution with an acid. Name the acid.

rejected.feedback: Hydrochloric acid would give potassium chloride.
Nitric acid would give potassium nitrate.

explanation: Sulfates are made from sulfuric acid: 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.

stem:
Excess zinc oxide is added to $25.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of $2.00\ \text{mol/dm}^3$ sulfuric acid. After filtering and crystallising, the student obtains $11.2\ \text{g}$ of zinc sulfate crystals, $\ce{ZnSO4.7H2O}$.

$$
\ce{ZnO + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2O}
$$

(Ar: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32, Zn = 65)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount, in moles, of sulfuric acid used.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of $\ce{ZnSO4.7H2O}$ crystals that could form.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** reasons why the yield is less than 100%.

points.description: Some zinc sulfate remains dissolved in the solution after crystallisation
Some solution/crystals are lost during filtering, transferring or washing
Some solution splashes out (spits) during heating (any two of D1-D3)

parts.explanation: Not all of the zinc sulfate crystallises: some stays dissolved in the cold solution. Some solution and crystals are also lost on the filter paper, on the apparatus and when the crystals are washed.

explanation: $n(\ce{H2SO4}) = 2.00 \times 0.0250 = 0.0500$ mol, giving at most $0.0500$ mol of crystals: $0.0500 \times 287 = 14.35\ \text{g}$. Percentage yield $= 11.2 \div 14.35 \times 100 = 78.0\%$.
workedSolution:
1. (a) $2.00 \times \dfrac{25.0}{1000} = 0.0500$ mol.
2. (b) Ratio $1 : 1$; $M_r = 287$; $0.0500 \times 287 = 14.35 \approx 14.4\ \text{g}$.
3. (c) $\dfrac{11.2}{14.35} \times 100 = 78.0\%$ (77.8% if 14.4 g is used).
4. (d) Salt left in solution; losses when filtering, transferring and washing.
hints: Convert cm³ to dm³ before using n = c × V.
Remember to include the 7 H₂O in the Mr of the crystals.

stem: Ammonium sulfate, a fertiliser, can be made in the laboratory by titrating aqueous ammonia with dilute sulfuric acid.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why ammonium sulfate cannot be made by adding excess aqueous ammonia and then filtering.

points.description: Aqueous ammonia is a solution / soluble (alkali), so the excess cannot be removed by filtering and would contaminate the salt

parts.explanation: Aqueous ammonia is a solution, so any excess stays dissolved with the salt and cannot be filtered off.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which indicator is suitable for finding the end-point of this titration?

options.rationale: Limewater tests for carbon dioxide.
A two-colour indicator gives a sharp colour change at the end-point.
This is a test for water, not an acid–base indicator.
Universal indicator changes gradually through many colours, so the end-point is not sharp.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: After finding the end-point, describe how the student obtains a solution of ammonium sulfate that is **not** contaminated with indicator.

points.description: Repeat the titration / mix the same volumes of acid and ammonia again
without adding the indicator (or: add activated charcoal to remove (adsorb) the indicator, then filter)

parts.explanation: She mixes the same volume of aqueous ammonia with the same volume of acid as before, but without indicator, so the solution contains only ammonium sulfate. (Alternatively, the indicator can be removed with activated charcoal and filtering.)

options.rationale: Ammonium ions are $\ce{NH4+}$, so two are needed for one $\ce{SO4^2-}$.
No water forms when ammonia (not a hydroxide) reacts with the acid; and this does not balance.
Two ammonia molecules each accept a proton from the acid.
No hydrogen gas is produced in neutralisation.

explanation: Aqueous ammonia is soluble, so the exact volumes are found by titration with an indicator such as methyl orange. The same volumes are then mixed without indicator and the solution is crystallised. $\ce{2NH3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4}$.
hints: Can a dissolved substance be filtered off?

stem: Describe how you would prepare pure, dry crystals of magnesium sulfate, starting from magnesium carbonate and dilute sulfuric acid. [6]

points.description: Add magnesium carbonate a little at a time to dilute sulfuric acid (in a beaker), stirring
Until it is in excess: fizzing stops and solid remains undissolved
Filter to remove the excess magnesium carbonate
Heat/evaporate the filtrate until the crystallisation point (crystals form on a cool glass rod)
Leave to cool so that crystals form; filter them off
Wash with a little cold distilled water and dry between filter papers (or in a warm place)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Pour some dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker. Add magnesium carbonate a spatula at a time, stirring, until the fizzing stops and some solid stays undissolved, which shows that the carbonate is in excess and all the acid has reacted. Filter the mixture to remove the excess magnesium carbonate. Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin until it reaches the crystallisation point (a drop on a cold glass rod forms crystals), then leave it to cool so that crystals of magnesium sulfate form. Filter off the crystals, wash them with a little cold distilled water and dry them between filter papers.

explanation: The essential stages are: excess insoluble carbonate, filtration, evaporation to the crystallisation point, cooling, and filtering, washing and drying the crystals.
hints: How will you know the carbonate is in excess?

stem: Why is the 'excess solid' method **not** used to make sodium chloride from sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid?

options.content: Sodium hydroxide is soluble, so excess could not be filtered off.
options.rationale: The excess alkali would stay in solution and contaminate the salt.

options.content: Sodium chloride decomposes when it is crystallised.
options.rationale: Sodium chloride crystallises without decomposing.

options.content: Sodium chloride is insoluble in water, so it is lost on the filter paper.
options.rationale: Sodium chloride is soluble; all sodium salts are.

options.content: Sodium hydroxide does not react with hydrochloric acid.
options.rationale: They react rapidly: it is a neutralisation.

explanation: The excess-solid method relies on filtering off the unreacted solid. An alkali dissolves, so instead the exact volumes are found by titration.
hints: Can you filter off something that has dissolved?

stem: Which metal is **unsuitable** for making its chloride by adding the metal to dilute hydrochloric acid, because the reaction would be dangerously violent?

options.rationale: Potassium is near the top of the reactivity series; it reacts explosively with acids.
Magnesium reacts vigorously but safely with dilute acids.
Zinc reacts at a steady, safe rate with dilute acids.
Iron reacts slowly and safely with dilute acids.

explanation: Metals high in the reactivity series (potassium, sodium, calcium) react dangerously with acids. Potassium chloride is made by titrating potassium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid instead.

stem: Excess zinc powder is stirred into blue copper(II) sulfate solution until the solution becomes colourless. The mixture is then filtered. What does the **filtrate** contain?

options.rationale: Zinc displaces copper: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
The zinc ions that replace the copper ions stay dissolved as zinc sulfate.
These are solids, left on the filter paper as the residue.
The blue colour disappeared, so the copper(II) ions have been removed.

explanation:
Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from its salt: $\ce{Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu}$. The residue is copper and the excess zinc; the filtrate is zinc sulfate solution, which can be crystallised.

*Syllabus note: preparing salts by displacement is ZIMSEC O-Level content.*
hints: Which metal ends up in solution?

stem: Copper(II) chloride is made from copper(II) carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid: $\ce{CuCO3 + 2HCl -> CuCl2 + H2O + CO2}$. Calculate the volume, in cm³, of $0.500\ \text{mol/dm}^3$ hydrochloric acid that reacts exactly with $1.24\ \text{g}$ of copper(II) carbonate. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Cu = 64)
hints: Use the 1 : 2 ratio of CuCO₃ to HCl.
V = n ÷ c gives dm³; multiply by 1000 for cm³.

stem: Thandeka's blue copper(II) sulfate crystals contain small black specks. Which mistake most likely caused this?

options.content: She washed the crystals with a little cold distilled water after filtering.
options.rationale: Washing with a little cold distilled water is the correct method.

options.content: She cooled the solution too slowly overnight.
options.rationale: Slow cooling gives larger crystals, not black specks.

options.content: Some excess copper(II) oxide got through because she filtered badly.
options.rationale: The black specks are unreacted copper(II) oxide.

options.content: She used too much sulfuric acid at the start.
options.rationale: Excess acid would leave the solution acidic, but it would not produce black solid.

explanation: Copper(II) oxide is black. If the excess is not completely removed by filtration (for example, a torn filter paper or liquid poured down the side of the paper), it ends up in the crystals.

stem: Which salt can be made by adding an excess of an insoluble base to a dilute acid, filtering, and crystallising the filtrate?

options.rationale: Excess copper(II) oxide with dilute nitric acid, then filter and crystallise.
A sodium salt: made by titration of sodium hydroxide with nitric acid.
Barium sulfate is insoluble: made by precipitation.
Silver chloride is insoluble: made by precipitation.

explanation: The salt must be soluble (so it can be crystallised) and not a sodium, potassium or ammonium salt. $\ce{CuO + 2HNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + H2O}$.
hints: The salt must be soluble, and its metal must come from an insoluble base.

stem: True or false: in the titration method for making a salt, the acid and alkali are mixed again in the same volumes **without** the indicator, so that the salt is not contaminated by the indicator.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: the first titration finds the volumes; the second mixture, without indicator, gives a pure salt solution.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: repeating without indicator (or removing the indicator with charcoal) stops it contaminating the salt.

explanation: The titration with indicator finds the exact volume of acid needed. Mixing the same volumes again without indicator gives a salt solution containing nothing else, which is then crystallised.
